slides.narration: Welcome to part one. An equation such as two x equals six has one answer, but an inequality such as two x is less than six has a whole set of answers. In this part you learn the rules for operating on an inequality, solve linear inequalities, and draw the answer on the number line.

slides.heading: Inequalities and solution sets
slides.body_md: A **linear inequality** in $x$ compares two expressions with $<$, $>$, $\le$ or $\ge$. Its **solution set** is every real number that makes it true. Strict signs leave the end point out; signs with a bar keep it in.

visual.alt: Table of the four inequality symbols: less than and greater than leave the end point out and use an open circle; at most and at least keep the end point and use a filled circle, each shown with the example x compared with 4.
visual.caption: A strict sign leaves the end point out; a sign with a bar keeps it in.

slides.narration: There are four signs. Less than and greater than are strict, so the end point is not part of the answer and we draw an open circle. At most and at least include the end point, so we draw a filled circle. The solution set is the collection of all real numbers that make the statement true, and it is usually an interval.

slides.heading: Drawing a solution set
slides.body_md: Shade the part of the line that belongs to the set. An **open circle** marks an end point that is left out, a **filled circle** one that is included, and an **arrow** shows that the set goes on for ever.

slides.heading: Rules for operating on an inequality
slides.body_md: Adding or subtracting the same number, and multiplying or dividing by a **positive** number, keep the sign. Multiplying or dividing by a **negative** number **reverses** it.

visual.alt: Table applying six operations to the true statement minus 2 less than 6: adding or subtracting a number, and multiplying or dividing by a positive number, keep the sign; multiplying or dividing by a negative number, minus 4 or minus 2, reverses it.
visual.caption: Only a negative multiplier or divisor reverses the sign.

slides.narration: Start from the true statement minus two is less than six. Adding five or subtracting seven keeps the sign. Multiplying by four, or dividing by two, also keeps it. But multiplying by minus four gives eight is greater than minus twenty four, and dividing by minus two gives one is greater than minus three. A negative multiplier turns the sign round.

slides.heading: Quick check: dividing by a negative number
slides.body_md: Decide whether a stated solution is correct.
slides.narration: Divide by minus two and reverse the sign.

slides.heading: The method, step by step
slides.body_md: Solving a linear inequality is like solving an equation, with one extra rule: when you divide by a negative coefficient of $x$, reverse the sign. Finish by checking a test value.

slides.narration: Collect the x terms on the left and the numbers on the right. Eight x minus three x is five x, and eighteen plus seven is twenty five. So five x is less than twenty five, and dividing by five gives x less than five. The circle at five is open because five itself is not allowed, and the shading runs to the left.

slides.heading: A negative coefficient reverses the sign
slides.body_md: When the coefficient of $x$ is negative, divide by it and **reverse** the sign. A common slip is to forget this step.

visual.alt: Table of three inequalities whose coefficient of x is negative: minus 3x plus 7 at least 22 gives x at most minus 5; 4 minus 5x less than 3x plus 20 gives x greater than minus 2; 10 minus 7x at least 24 gives x at most minus 2; the sign is reversed each time.
visual.caption: A negative coefficient of $x$ reverses the sign when we divide.

slides.narration: These three inequalities all end with a negative coefficient. Minus three x is at least fifteen becomes x is at most minus five. Minus eight x is less than sixteen becomes x is greater than minus two. Minus seven x is at least fourteen becomes x is at most minus two. In every row the sign is reversed when we divide by the negative number.

slides.body_md: Solve $\dfrac{3x - 1}{4} - \dfrac{x + 2}{3} \le \dfrac{1}{2}$.
bullets: Multiply by the least common multiple $12$ (positive, sign kept)

visual.alt: Worked example 2 table: multiply the inequality with fractions by 12, expand to get 9x minus 3 minus 4x minus 8 at most 6, collect to 5x at most 17, and divide by 5 to get x at most 17 over 5.
visual.caption: Multiplying by a positive LCM keeps the sign.

slides.narration: To clear the fractions multiply every term by twelve, the least common multiple of four, three and two. Because twelve is positive the sign stays. We get three times three x minus one, minus four times x plus two, is at most six. Expanding gives five x minus eleven is at most six, so five x is at most seventeen, and x is at most seventeen over five.

slides.body_md: A double inequality such as $1 < x \le 6$ gives two conditions at once. To solve one, do each operation on **all three parts**; if you divide by a negative number, reverse **both** signs.

visual.caption: Open circles mark end points that are left out, filled circles mark end points that are included, and an arrow shows that the set goes on for ever.

slides.narration: A double inequality says that x is between two numbers. Here x is greater than one and at most six. On the line the circle at one is open and the circle at six is filled, with the shading between. When solving, whatever you do to the middle you must do to both ends, and if you divide by a negative number both signs must be reversed.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a double inequality
slides.body_md: Solve $-4 \le \dfrac{7 - 3x}{2} < 5$.
bullets: Divide by $-3$, reversing both signs: $5 \ge x > -1$

rows: Divide all parts by $-3$ and reverse both signs

visual.alt: Worked example 3 table: minus 4 at most 7 minus 3x over 2, less than 5; multiplying by 2 gives minus 8 at most 7 minus 3x less than 10; subtracting 7 gives minus 15 at most minus 3x less than 3; dividing by minus 3 reverses both signs and gives x in the interval from minus 1, left out, to 5, included.
visual.caption: Operate on all three parts; reverse both signs if you divide by a negative number.

slides.narration: Multiply all three parts by two to get minus eight, then seven minus three x, then ten. Subtract seven from every part. Now divide every part by minus three. The signs reverse, so minus fifteen over minus three becomes five, and three over minus three becomes minus one. Written in the usual order, x is greater than minus one and at most five.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading a number line
slides.body_md: Read an interval from a picture.
slides.narration: Look at each circle: filled means included, open means left out.

slides.heading: Three possible outcomes
slides.body_md: If the $x$ terms cancel, what is left is a true or a false numerical statement. **False**: no solution. **True**: every real number. Otherwise the solution is a ray.

visual.alt: Table of three outcomes: five times x minus 2 greater than 5x minus 7 reduces to 0 greater than 3, which is false, so there is no solution; 4x plus 9 at least twice 2x plus 3 reduces to 0 at least minus 3, which is true, so every real number works; 3x minus 5 at most 2x plus 1 gives x at most 6.
visual.caption: If the $x$ terms cancel, the truth of what is left decides everything.

slides.narration: Sometimes the x terms cancel. In the first row we are left with zero is greater than three, which is false, so no real number works. In the second row we are left with zero is at least minus three, which is true, so every real number works. In the third row we get a ray, x at most six. The truth of what remains decides everything.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a word problem
slides.body_md: An imagined canteen plan costs ₹150 plus ₹8 per meal; paying per meal costs ₹14. For how many meals is the plan cheaper?
bullets: Let $n$ be the number of meals: $150 + 8n < 14n$
$n$ is a whole number, so the least value is $26$

rows: Let $n$ be the number of meals

visual.alt: Worked example 4 table for an imagined canteen plan: 150 plus 8n rupees against 14n rupees; the plan is cheaper when 150 plus 8n is less than 14n, so n is greater than 25 and the least whole number is 26, checked by the costs 350 and 350 at 25 meals and 358 and 364 at 26 meals.
visual.caption: Read the answer back in words, and respect whole numbers.

slides.narration: Let n be the number of meals. The plan costs one hundred fifty plus eight n, and paying per meal costs fourteen n. The plan is cheaper when one hundred fifty plus eight n is less than fourteen n. That gives one hundred fifty less than six n, so n is greater than twenty five. Twenty five meals cost the same, so the least whole number is twenty six.

slides.heading: Quick check: a whole-number answer
slides.body_md: Find the least integer in a solution set.
slides.narration: The end point itself is left out, so look at the next integer.

Solve like an equation, then write an interval and draw the set
Double inequality: work on all three parts

decks.title: Linear and Quadratic Inequalities - Part 2: quadratic and rational inequalities
goals: Use the sign of a quadratic and the method of intervals to solve quadratic inequalities
Solve inequalities with perfect squares and quadratics with no real roots
Solve rational inequalities compared with a constant, excluding values that make the denominator zero
Decide which end points belong to the solution set

slides.heading: Quadratic and Rational Inequalities
slides.body_md: Where is a quadratic positive, and where is a fraction negative?

nodes.label: Sign of a quadratic
Method of intervals
Perfect squares and no real roots
Rational inequalities
End points

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the sign of a quadratic, the method of intervals, perfect squares and quadratics with no real roots, rational inequalities compared with a constant, and the rules for end points.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Linear inequalities have rays as answers. Quadratic inequalities can have two rays, or an interval, or even a single point. In this part you learn the method of intervals, meet perfect squares and quadratics with no real roots, and finish with rational inequalities, where the denominator needs special care.

slides.heading: The sign of a quadratic
slides.body_md: The graph of $y = x^2 - 3x - 10$ is above the $x$-axis where the expression is positive and below it where it is negative. The sign can change only at a root.

visual.alt: Graph of y equal to x squared minus 3x minus 10: an upward parabola crossing the x-axis at minus 2 and 5, with lowest point (1.5, minus 12.25) and y-intercept minus 10. The curve is above the axis for x less than minus 2 and for x greater than 5, and below it between the two crossings.
visual.caption: Above the axis outside the roots, below it between them.

slides.narration: This parabola opens upwards and crosses the x axis at minus two and at five. To the left of minus two and to the right of five the curve is above the axis, so the quadratic is positive there. Between the two roots the curve is below the axis, so it is negative. The sign can change only at a root.

slides.heading: The method of intervals
slides.body_md: Bring everything to one side and compare with $0$. Factorise, mark the **critical points** on a number line, find the sign in each region, then choose the regions and decide the end points.

nodes.label: Move everything to one side; compare with $0$
Factorise
Mark the critical points on a number line
Find the sign in each region
Pick the regions; decide each end point

visual.alt: Flow chart of the method of intervals: move everything to one side so the other side is zero, factorise, mark the critical points on a number line, find the sign of the expression in each region, then choose the regions and decide each end point.
visual.caption: The sign can only change at a critical point.

slides.narration: Here is the method. Move every term to one side so that the other side is zero. Factorise. Mark the critical points, which are the zeros of the factors, on a number line. They split the line into regions, and in each region the expression has one sign. Choose the regions you need, and decide whether each critical point is included.

slides.heading: A sign chart
slides.body_md: $x^2 - 3x - 10 = (x + 2)(x - 5) \ge 0$. Multiply the signs of the factors region by region; the critical points $-2$ and $5$ give $0$, which is allowed by $\ge$.

visual.alt: Sign chart for x squared minus 3x minus 10, which factorises as x plus 2 times x minus 5, with the critical points minus 2 and 5: the product is positive for x less than minus 2, negative between minus 2 and 5, and positive for x greater than 5, so the inequality at least 0 holds in the first and third regions.
visual.caption: The signs of the two factors multiply; the end points $-2$ and $5$ give $0$, which is allowed by $\ge$.

slides.narration: The expression factorises as x plus two times x minus five. For x less than minus two both factors are negative, so the product is positive. Between minus two and five the factors have opposite signs, so the product is negative. Beyond five both are positive. For at least zero we take the first and last regions and include both critical points.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: between the roots

visual.alt: Worked example 1 sign chart for 2x squared minus 5x minus 3, which is 2x plus 1 times x minus 3, with critical points minus one half and 3: the product is negative only between them, so the strict inequality less than 0 gives the open interval from minus one half to 3.
visual.caption: Both end points give $0$, which is not less than $0$, so they stay out.

slides.narration: Factorise two x squared minus five x minus three as two x plus one times x minus three. The critical points are minus one half and three. The product is negative when the two factors have opposite signs, which happens only between the critical points. The inequality is strict, so both end points stay out, and the solution is the open interval from minus one half to three.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading the sign
slides.body_md: Say where a product of two factors is negative.
slides.narration: Opposite signs between the roots.

slides.heading: The leading coefficient decides the pattern
slides.body_md: Make the coefficient of $x^2$ **positive** first (multiply by $-1$ and reverse the sign). Then a positive quadratic is positive outside the roots and negative between them.

visual.alt: Table linking the leading coefficient to the shape: for a greater than 0 the parabola opens upwards, the quadratic is positive outside the roots and negative between them; for a less than 0 it opens downwards, positive between the roots and negative outside.
visual.caption: Two real roots: the sign pattern depends only on the sign of $a$.

slides.narration: If the leading coefficient is positive the parabola opens upwards. It is positive outside the roots and negative between them. If it is negative the pattern is the other way round. The safest habit is to make the leading coefficient positive first, by multiplying the whole inequality by minus one, and then reversing the sign.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a negative leading coefficient

rows: Multiply by $-1$ and reverse the sign

visual.alt: Worked example 2 table: twelve minus x minus x squared greater than 0 is rewritten with a positive x squared by multiplying by minus 1 and reversing the sign, giving x squared plus x minus 12 less than 0, which factorises as x plus 4 times x minus 3, so the solution is the open interval from minus 4 to 3, and x equal 0 checks.
visual.caption: Make the leading coefficient positive, and reverse the sign.

slides.narration: The leading coefficient is negative, so first multiply by minus one and reverse the sign. We get x squared plus x minus twelve is less than zero. Factorise as x plus four times x minus three. A positive quadratic is negative between its roots, so the solution is x between minus four and three. Check with x equal to zero: twelve is greater than zero, which is true.

slides.heading: Quick check: a square
slides.body_md: Decide whether a stated solution set is correct.
slides.narration: Test a value between the roots.

slides.heading: Perfect squares
slides.body_md: A perfect square never changes sign. $(x - 3)^2$ is positive except at $x = 3$, where it is $0$. So "$\le 0$" gives a single point and "$< 0$" gives nothing.

rows: a square is positive except at its root
a square is zero only at its root

visual.alt: Table of the four inequalities for the perfect square x minus 3 all squared: at least 0 holds for every real number, greater than 0 holds for every real number except 3, at most 0 holds only at 3, and less than 0 has no solution.
visual.caption: The sign of a perfect square never changes.

slides.narration: A perfect square is never negative. So x minus three squared is at least zero for every real number, and it is greater than zero for every real number except three. It is at most zero only at x equal to three, which gives a single point, and it is never less than zero, which gives the empty set. The sign never changes, so there is no sign chart to draw.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: recognise the square

visual.alt: Worked example 3 table: four x squared plus 12x plus 9 is the perfect square 2x plus 3 all squared with root minus three halves; greater than 0 holds for every real number except minus three halves, and at most 0 holds only at minus three halves.
visual.caption: Same expression, opposite verdicts at the root.

slides.narration: Look at the first and last terms. Four x squared is two x squared, and nine is three squared, and the middle term is twice two x times three. So the expression is two x plus three, all squared. Its root is minus three halves. It is positive everywhere except at that root, and it is at most zero only at that root.

slides.heading: Quadratics with no real roots
slides.body_md: If the discriminant $D = b^2 - 4ac$ is **negative**, the quadratic has the sign of $a$ for every real $x$. Here $D = -12$ and $a > 0$, so $x^2 - 2x + 4 > 0$ always.

visual.alt: Graph of y equal to x squared minus 2x plus 4: an upward parabola with lowest point (1, 3) and y-intercept 4. It never reaches the x-axis because the discriminant is minus 12, so the quadratic is positive for every real x.
visual.caption: Discriminant $-12 < 0$: the curve stays above the axis.

slides.narration: This parabola has its lowest point at one comma three, above the axis, so it never crosses. The discriminant is negative, minus twelve. When the discriminant is negative there is no real root, so the quadratic keeps the sign of its leading coefficient everywhere. Here that sign is positive, so the quadratic is greater than zero for every real number and less than zero for none.

slides.heading: Quick check: a negative discriminant
slides.body_md: Complete the statement about all real numbers.
slides.narration: Find the discriminant first.

slides.heading: Rational inequalities: the plan
slides.body_md: To solve $\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ compared with a constant, **move the constant across** so one side is $0$, combine into a single fraction, factorise and use a sign chart. **Never include a zero of the denominator.**

nodes.label: Move the constant across: one side is zero
Combine into a single fraction
Factorise top and bottom
Mark zeros of the top and of the bottom
Sign chart; never include a zero of the bottom

visual.alt: Flow chart for a rational inequality: move the constant across so that one side is zero, combine into a single fraction, factorise the top and the bottom, mark the zeros of both, then use a sign chart and never include a zero of the bottom.
visual.caption: Never multiply across by a denominator whose sign you do not know.

slides.narration: For an inequality with a fraction compared with a number, do not multiply across. Move the number to the other side so that one side is zero, then combine into a single fraction. Factorise the top and the bottom. Mark the zeros of both, and use a sign chart. Zeros of the bottom are never part of the answer, because division by zero is not allowed.

slides.heading: A tempting wrong method
slides.body_md: Multiplying $\dfrac{x - 1}{x + 2} \ge 3$ by $x + 2$ as if it were positive gives $x \le -\dfrac{7}{2}$. The test values show that this is wrong.

visual.alt: Table testing the wrong set x at most minus 7 over 2, obtained by multiplying x minus 1 over x plus 2 at least 3 by x plus 2 as if it were positive: x equal minus 4 gives 5 over 2, which fails, yet it is in the wrong set; x equal minus 3 gives 4, which works, yet it is outside the wrong set.
visual.caption: Multiplying by $x + 2$ is only allowed when its sign is known.

slides.narration: Suppose we multiply by x plus two as though it were positive. We get x minus one is at least three x plus six, and so x is at most minus seven halves. Now test. At minus four the fraction is five halves, which is less than three, yet minus four is in the wrong set. At minus three the fraction is four, which works, yet minus three is outside it. The multiplication was not allowed.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a fraction against a constant
slides.body_md: Solve $\dfrac{3x - 2}{x + 1} \le 2$.
bullets: Negative between them; $4$ gives $0$ (included), $-1$ is excluded

visual.alt: Worked example 4 sign chart. The inequality 3x minus 2 over x plus 1 at most 2 becomes x minus 4 over x plus 1 at most 0 after subtracting 2. The critical points are minus 1 and 4: the fraction is positive for x less than minus 1, negative between minus 1 and 4, and positive after 4, so the solution is minus 1 excluded up to 4 included.
visual.caption: The zero of the top, $4$, is included; the zero of the bottom, $-1$, never is.

slides.narration: Subtract two from both sides and combine into one fraction. The top becomes three x minus two minus two x minus two, which is x minus four. So we need x minus four over x plus one to be at most zero. The critical points are four and minus one. The fraction is negative between them. At four the value is zero, so four is included, but minus one is excluded.

slides.heading: Quick check: a wrong shortcut
slides.body_md: Decide whether a shortcut is valid.
slides.narration: Think about the sign of x minus three.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: quadratics top and bottom
slides.body_md: Solve $\dfrac{x^2 - x - 6}{x^2 - 1} \ge 0$.
bullets: Signs alternate across the four points: $+, -, +, -, +$
Include the zeros of the top; exclude those of the bottom

visual.alt: Worked example 5 sign chart for x squared minus x minus 6 over x squared minus 1, that is x plus 2 times x minus 3 over x plus 1 times x minus 1, with critical points minus 2, minus 1, 1 and 3. The fraction is positive for x less than minus 2, negative, positive between minus 1 and 1, negative, and positive for x greater than 3.
visual.caption: Zeros of the top, $-2$ and $3$, are included; zeros of the bottom, $-1$ and $1$, are not.

slides.narration: Factorise the top as x plus two times x minus three, and the bottom as x plus one times x minus one. The critical points are minus two, minus one, one and three. The fraction is positive for x less than minus two, then the signs alternate, so it is positive between minus one and one, and positive beyond three. Include minus two and three, which make the top zero, and exclude minus one and one.

slides.heading: Which end points belong?
slides.body_md: A zero of the **top** is included only when the sign is $\ge$ or $\le$. A zero of the **bottom** is **never** included.

visual.alt: Table of the two critical points of x minus 4 over x plus 1 for the inequality at least 0: at x equal 4 the value is 0 and the point is in the solution; at x equal minus 1 the value is undefined and the point is never in the solution.
visual.caption: Zeros of the top follow the sign; zeros of the bottom are always out.

slides.narration: Take x minus four over x plus one, at least zero. At x equal to four the top is zero, so the value is zero, and at least zero allows it. At x equal to minus one the bottom is zero, so the fraction is undefined and the point can never be in the answer. A strict sign leaves out the zeros of the top as well.

slides.heading: Quick check: an excluded value
slides.body_md: Name the value that must be excluded.
slides.narration: Set the denominator equal to zero.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Quadratic: factorise, mark the critical points, read the signs
Positive leading coefficient: positive **outside** the roots, negative **between** them
Perfect square or $D < 0$: the sign never changes
Rational: one side zero, sign chart, **never** include a zero of the bottom

nodes.label: Quadratic: factorise, critical points, sign chart
Positive leading coefficient: outside or between the roots
Perfect square and negative discriminant: constant sign
Rational: one side zero, never include a zero of the bottom

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 2: a quadratic inequality is solved with factors, critical points and a sign chart; with a positive leading coefficient the answer is outside or between the roots; a perfect square or a negative discriminant gives a constant sign; a rational inequality is brought to one side and never includes a zero of the bottom.
visual.caption: Part 2 in four steps.

slides.narration: To sum up. A quadratic inequality is solved by factorising, marking the critical points and reading the signs. With a positive leading coefficient the quadratic is positive outside the roots and negative between them. A perfect square, or a negative discriminant, never changes sign. A rational inequality is brought to one side, and the zeros of the denominator are never included.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Say which end points are **in** and **why**
Never multiply by an expression of **unknown sign**
Test **one value** in the answer and one outside it

rows: factors 1, sign chart 1, set with end points 1
recognising the square or the discriminant 1, set 1
one side zero 1, critical points and chart 1, set with the pole out 1

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 2: a quadratic inequality earns factors, a sign chart and the set with end points; a perfect square or negative discriminant earns the recognition and the set; a rational inequality earns one side zero, the chart and the set with the pole left out; a common part earns each set and the intersection.
visual.caption: Always say which end points are in and why.

slides.narration: In the examination, make the leading coefficient positive before you read off the answer. Say which end points are included and why, because that carries a mark. Never multiply across by an expression whose sign you do not know. And finish by testing one value inside your answer and one value outside it.

notes.title: Linear and Quadratic Inequalities - chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Inequalities, solution sets and the number line
sections.body_md:
An **inequality** compares two expressions with $<$, $>$, $\le$ or $\ge$. A **linear inequality in one variable** has the form $ax + b < cx + d$ (or with another sign). Its **solution set** is the set of real numbers that make it true; it is written as an interval.

**Number line:** shade the set; an **open circle** marks an end point that is left out (strict sign), a **filled circle** one that is included, and an **arrow** shows that the set continues for ever. The symbol $\infty$ never gets a bracket that includes it: write $(-\infty, 5]$ and $[2, \infty)$.

**Interval notation:** $(a, b)$ both ends out, $[a, b]$ both in, $[a, b)$ and $(a, b]$ one in. Combining two sets: **and** gives the common part, **or** gives everything in either.

key_terms.definition_md: All real numbers that make the inequality true.
One with $<$ or $>$; the end point is left out.
A set such as $(a, b)$, $[a, b]$, $(a, \infty)$ written with brackets.

sections.heading: 2. Rules and the method for linear inequalities
sections.body_md:
**Rules.** Adding or subtracting the same number, and multiplying or dividing by a **positive** number, keep the sign. Multiplying or dividing by a **negative** number **reverses** the sign.

**Method.** Clear brackets and fractions (multiply by the positive least common multiple); collect the $x$ terms on one side and numbers on the other; divide by the coefficient of $x$ (reverse the sign if it is negative); write the interval and draw it; check one value inside and one outside.

Example: $-3x + 7 \ge 22$ gives $-3x \ge 15$, so $x \le -5$ (sign reversed).

key_terms.definition_md: Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number turns $<$ into $>$ and $\le$ into $\ge$.

sections.heading: 3. Double inequalities, special cases and word problems
sections.body_md:
**Double inequality.** $p < f(x) \le q$ means two conditions at once. Operate on **all three parts**; if you divide by a negative number reverse **both** signs, then write the result in increasing order, for example $5 \ge x > -1$ is $-1 < x \le 5$.

**Special cases.** If the $x$ terms cancel, a false statement (such as $0 > 3$) means **no solution** ($\varnothing$) and a true statement (such as $0 \ge -3$) means **every real number**.

**Word problems.** Define the variable, form the inequality, solve, and read the answer back in words; for counts take whole numbers only (for $n > 25$ the least whole number is $26$).

key_terms.definition_md: A statement $p < f(x) < q$ (or with $\le$) with an expression between two bounds.
$\varnothing$: the solution set when no number satisfies the inequality.

sections.heading: 4. Quadratic inequalities by the method of intervals
sections.body_md:
To solve $ax^2 + bx + c \ \square\ 0$ (with $\square$ one of the four signs): 1) bring all terms to one side so the other side is $0$; 2) factorise; 3) mark the **critical points** (the roots) on a number line; 4) find the sign of the expression in each region by multiplying the signs of the factors (the signs alternate when every root is simple); 5) pick the regions with the right sign and decide each end point.

For $a > 0$ and two real roots $\alpha < \beta$: $ax^2 + bx + c > 0$ for $x < \alpha$ or $x > \beta$ (**outside** the roots) and $< 0$ for $\alpha < x < \beta$ (**between** the roots). With $\ge$ or $\le$ the roots are included. Example: $x^2 - 3x - 10 \ge 0$ gives $(-\infty, -2] \cup [5, \infty)$.

key_terms.definition_md: A value where a factor is zero; the sign of the expression can change only there.
Solving by marking the critical points and finding the sign in each region.

sections.heading: 5. Negative leading coefficient, perfect squares and no real roots
sections.body_md:
**Negative leading coefficient.** Multiply by $-1$ and reverse the sign first: $12 - x - x^2 > 0$ becomes $x^2 + x - 12 < 0$, giving $(-4, 3)$.

**Perfect squares.** $(x - k)^2 \ge 0$ for all real $x$; $(x - k)^2 > 0$ except at $x = k$; $(x - k)^2 \le 0$ only at $x = k$ (the solution set is the single point $\{k\}$); $(x - k)^2 < 0$ has no solution. Recognise squares such as $4x^2 + 12x + 9 = (2x + 3)^2$.

**No real roots.** If $D = b^2 - 4ac < 0$ the quadratic has the sign of $a$ for every real $x$: for $a > 0$ it is always positive, so $> 0$ gives $\mathbb{R}$ and $< 0$ gives $\varnothing$. Conditions such as "$ax^2 + bx + c > 0$ for every real $x$" mean $a > 0$ and $D < 0$.

sections.heading: 6. Rational inequalities compared with a constant
sections.body_md:
To solve $\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)} \ \square\ k$: move $k$ across so one side is $0$, combine into a single fraction $\dfrac{f(x) - kg(x)}{g(x)}$, factorise top and bottom, mark the zeros of both, and use a sign chart.

**Never multiply across by $g(x)$** unless its sign is known: if it is negative the sign must reverse, and it changes sign at its zeros. Example: $\dfrac{3x - 2}{x + 1} \le 2$ becomes $\dfrac{x - 4}{x + 1} \le 0$, with solution $(-1, 4]$.

**End points.** A zero of the **top** is included only for $\ge$ or $\le$. A zero of the **bottom** is **never** included, whatever the sign. A square factor in the top gives an isolated zero without a sign change; for example $\dfrac{(x - 1)^2}{x + 2} \le 0$ has the solution $(-\infty, -2) \cup \{1\}$.

sections.heading: 7. Combining conditions
sections.body_md:
When two conditions must both hold, take the **common part** (intersection) of their solution sets; for **either** condition, take the **union**. Draw each set on its own number line and read off the overlap, watching the end points: a point is in the common part only if both sets contain it.

Example: $x^2 - x - 12 \le 0$ gives $[-3, 4]$ and $\dfrac{x + 1}{x - 6} < 0$ gives $(-1, 6)$; both hold on $(-1, 4]$. Quadratic inequalities in a parameter (for example "for what $k$ is $x^2 - 2kx + 3k + 4 > 0$ for all $x$?") reduce to a quadratic inequality in $k$ through the discriminant.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are usually awarded**
- *Linear inequality (2-3 marks):* collecting terms, the sign reversal when dividing by a negative number, the set (and its graph).
- *Double inequality (3 marks):* working on all three parts, reversing both signs, the interval.
- *Quadratic inequality (2-3 marks):* factorising, critical points with a sign chart, the set with the correct end points.
- *Perfect square or $D < 0$ (2 marks):* recognising the square or finding the discriminant, the set (a point, $\varnothing$ or $\mathbb{R}$).
- *Rational inequality (3 marks):* one side zero, critical points and chart, the set with the zeros of the bottom left out.
- *Section D (5 marks):* parts such as 3 + 2; label each part, and give the common part of two sets in the last step.

**Common mistakes**
1. Not reversing the sign when dividing or multiplying by a negative number.
2. Using a filled circle for a strict sign, or an open circle for $\le$ and $\ge$.
3. Solving $x^2 \ge 16$ as $x \ge 4$ and missing $x \le -4$.
4. Forgetting to make the leading coefficient positive before reading "outside" or "between".
5. Multiplying a rational inequality by the denominator without knowing its sign.
6. Including a zero of the denominator in the solution set.
7. Treating $(x - 1)^2 \le 0$ as having no solution, or $(x - 1)^2 > 0$ as true for all $x$.
8. Giving a decimal count (for example $25.5$ meals) instead of a whole number.

cards.front_md: What is the solution set of an inequality?
cards.back_md: The set of all real numbers that make the inequality true; written as an interval.

cards.front_md: Which signs include the end point?
cards.back_md: $\le$ and $\ge$ (filled circle); $<$ and $>$ leave it out (open circle).

cards.front_md: Rule for multiplying both sides by a negative number?
cards.back_md: Reverse the sign: $a < b$ and $c < 0$ give $ac > bc$.

cards.front_md: Does adding a number to both sides change the sign?
cards.back_md: No: adding or subtracting the same number keeps the sign.

cards.front_md: Solve $-3x \ge 12$.
cards.back_md: Divide by $-3$ and reverse: $x \le -4$, that is $(-\infty, -4]$.

cards.front_md: First step for an inequality with fractions?
cards.back_md: Multiply by the positive least common multiple of the denominators; the sign is kept.

cards.front_md: Write $x > 2$ and $x \le 7$ together as an interval.
How do you solve a double inequality?
cards.back_md: Work on all three parts; if you divide by a negative number reverse both signs.

cards.front_md: What does $0 > 3$ left after cancelling $x$ mean?
cards.back_md: A false statement: no solution, $\varnothing$.

cards.front_md: What does $0 \ge -3$ left after cancelling $x$ mean?
cards.back_md: A true statement: every real number, $\mathbb{R}$.

cards.front_md: How do you read a word problem answer for a count?
cards.back_md: Take whole numbers only: for $n > 25$ the least value is $26$.

cards.front_md: What is a critical point?
cards.back_md: A value where a factor is zero; the sign of the expression can change only there.

cards.front_md: First step for a quadratic inequality?
cards.back_md: Bring all terms to one side so the other side is zero, then factorise.

cards.front_md: $a > 0$ and roots $\alpha < \beta$: where is $ax^2 + bx + c < 0$?
cards.back_md: Between the roots: $\alpha < x < \beta$.

cards.front_md: $a > 0$: where is $ax^2 + bx + c > 0$?
cards.back_md: Outside the roots: $x < \alpha$ or $x > \beta$.

cards.front_md: Solve $x^2 - 3x - 10 \ge 0$.
What if the leading coefficient is negative?
cards.back_md: Multiply by $-1$ and reverse the sign, then use the pattern for $a > 0$.

cards.front_md: Solution of $(x - k)^2 \ge 0$?
cards.back_md: Every real number.

cards.front_md: Solution of $(x - k)^2 > 0$?
cards.back_md: Every real number except $k$.

cards.front_md: Solution of $(x - k)^2 \le 0$ and of $(x - k)^2 < 0$?
cards.back_md: $\{k\}$ and $\varnothing$.

cards.front_md: What does $D < 0$ say about $ax^2 + bx + c$?
cards.back_md: No real root: it has the sign of $a$ for every real $x$.

cards.front_md: Condition for $ax^2 + bx + c > 0$ for all real $x$?
First step for $\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ compared with a constant?
cards.back_md: Move the constant across so one side is $0$ and combine into one fraction.

cards.front_md: Why not multiply across by the denominator?
cards.back_md: Its sign may be negative (the sign would reverse) and it changes sign at its zero.

cards.front_md: Is a zero of the denominator ever in the solution set?
cards.back_md: Never: the expression is undefined there.

cards.front_md: Is a zero of the numerator in the solution set?
cards.back_md: Only for $\ge$ or $\le$ (the value is $0$); not for a strict sign.

cards.front_md: Solve $\dfrac{3x - 2}{x + 1} \le 2$.
What does a square factor in the numerator do?
cards.back_md: It gives a zero without a sign change; the zero can be an isolated solution.

cards.front_md: Meaning of "and" and "or" for two conditions?
cards.back_md: "And": the common part (intersection); "or": the union.

cards.front_md: Solve $x^2 \ge 16$.
cards.back_md: $(x - 4)(x + 4) \ge 0$: $(-\infty, -4] \cup [4, \infty)$, not just $x \ge 4$.

questions.stem_md: Both sides of the true statement $-3 < 5$ are multiplied by $-2$. The statement that results is
questions.solution_md: Multiplying by a negative number reverses the sign: $(-3)(-2) = 6$ and $(5)(-2) = -10$, so $6 > -10$. Option (b) keeps the old sign, which makes a false statement.

questions.stem_md: For real $x$, the inequality $7x - 4 > 2x + 21$ is true exactly for
questions.solution_md: Collect the $x$ terms: $7x - 2x > 21 + 4$, so $5x > 25$ and $x > 5$, which is $(5, \infty)$. Option (d) includes the end point $5$, but $x = 5$ gives $31 > 31$, which is false.

questions.stem_md: Over the real numbers, the inequality $11 - 3x \ge 2x - 4$ is satisfied by exactly
questions.solution_md: Collect: $11 + 4 \ge 2x + 3x$, so $15 \ge 5x$ and $x \le 3$. Option (d) divides by the positive number $5$ but still turns the sign round; option (a) is the set for $x \ge -3$.

questions.stem_md: The number of integers $x$ that satisfy the double inequality $-7 \le 3x - 1 < 11$ is
questions.solution_md: Add $1$ to every part: $-6 \le 3x < 12$. Divide every part by $3$: $-2 \le x < 4$. The integers are $-2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3$, which is $6$ of them. Option (b) counts the end point $4$, which is left out.

questions.stem_md: The number line below shows the solution set of an inequality in the real number $x$. Which statement describes exactly this set?
questions.solution_md: The circle at $-2$ is filled, so $-2$ belongs to the set; the circle at $5$ is open, so $5$ does not. The set is $-2 \le x < 5$. Option (b) swaps the two end points.

questions.stem_md: The greatest integer that satisfies $\dfrac{2x + 1}{3} - \dfrac{x - 2}{2} < 2$ is
questions.solution_md: Multiply by $6$: $2(2x + 1) - 3(x - 2) < 12$, so $4x + 2 - 3x + 6 < 12$ and $x + 8 < 12$, giving $x < 4$. The end point $4$ is left out, so the greatest integer is $3$.

questions.stem_md: The inequality $kx + 6 > 18$, with $k$ a non-zero constant, has exactly the same solution set as $x < -3$. The value of $k$ is
questions.solution_md: $kx > 12$. The solution points to the left ($x < -3$), so the sign was reversed and $k$ is negative. Then $x < \dfrac{12}{k}$, and $\dfrac{12}{k} = -3$ gives $k = -4$. Check: $-4x + 6 > 18$ gives $-4x > 12$, so $x < -3$.

questions.stem_md: The inequality $(x - 4)(x + 1) < 0$ is true for exactly those real numbers $x$ that lie
questions.solution_md: The critical points are $-1$ and $4$. A product of two factors is negative when the factors have opposite signs, which happens only between the roots: $-1 < x < 4$.

questions.stem_md: The solution set of $x^2 - 7x + 10 \le 0$ is
questions.solution_md: $x^2 - 7x + 10 = (x - 2)(x - 5)$. The parabola opens upwards, so it is negative or zero between the roots, and the roots are included because of $\le$: $[2, 5]$. Option (b) is the set for $\ge 0$.

questions.stem_md: For real $x$, the inequality $x^2 - 9 > 0$ holds for

For $x < -2$ the bottom is negative, so the fraction is negative and satisfies $\le 0$. For $x > -2$ and $x \ne 1$ the fraction is positive. At $x = 1$ the top is $0$, so the value is $0$, which is allowed by $\le$. The point $-2$ is excluded (denominator $0$). The solution set is $(-\infty, -2) \cup \{1\}$; the value $1$ belongs because the fraction is $0$ there although it is positive on both sides.

questions.solution_md: A square factor does not change the sign but still gives a zero.

questions.stem_md: Aman solves $\dfrac{x + 1}{x - 2} \ge 2$ by multiplying both sides by $x - 2$ to get $x + 1 \ge 2x - 4$, and answers $x \le 5$. Show with a test value that his answer is wrong, and give the correct solution set.

answer.model_answer_md: Take $x = 1$, which is in his set $x \le 5$. Then $\dfrac{x + 1}{x - 2} = \dfrac{2}{-1} = -2$, and $-2 \ge 2$ is false, so his answer is wrong. He multiplied by $x - 2$ without knowing its sign. Correct method: $\dfrac{x + 1}{x - 2} - 2 = \dfrac{5 - x}{x - 2} \ge 0$, that is $\dfrac{x - 5}{x - 2} \le 0$. The critical points are $2$ (excluded) and $5$ (included), and the fraction is negative between them. The solution set is $(2, 5]$.

questions.stem_md: The solution set of $x^2 + px + q \le 0$ over the real numbers is the closed interval $[-2, 5]$. Find the numbers $p$ and $q$.

answer.model_answer_md: A quadratic with leading coefficient $1$ is $\le 0$ between its roots, so the roots are $x = -2$ and $x = 5$. Then $x^2 + px + q = (x + 2)(x - 5) = x^2 - 3x - 10$. Comparing coefficients, $p = -3$ and $q = -10$. Check with $x = 0$: $-10 \le 0$ is true, while $x = 6$ gives $36 - 18 - 10 = 8 > 0$.

questions.solution_md: The end points of the interval are the roots.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts.

(a) Solve $2x^2 - 7x - 4 \le 0$ for real $x$, using a sign chart. [3]

(b) List the integers that satisfy the inequality and find their sum. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Factorise: $2x^2 - 7x - 4 = (2x + 1)(x - 4)$. The critical points are $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $x = 4$. Sign chart: for $x < -\dfrac{1}{2}$ both factors are negative, so the product is positive; between the points the product is negative; for $x > 4$ both factors are positive. We need $\le 0$, so we take the middle region with both end points. The solution set is $[-\dfrac{1}{2}, 4]$.

(b) The integers in $-\dfrac{1}{2} \le x \le 4$ are $0, 1, 2, 3, 4$. Their sum is $0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10$.

questions.stem_md:
In an imagined demonstration, a model rocket has height $h = 30t - 5t^2$ metres at time $t$ seconds, for $0 \le t \le 6$.

(a) For which values of $t$ is the rocket at least $40$ m above the ground? [3]

(b) Show that the rocket never reaches a height of $50$ m. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) We need $30t - 5t^2 \ge 40$, so $5t^2 - 30t + 40 \le 0$, that is $t^2 - 6t + 8 \le 0$. Factorise: $(t - 2)(t - 4) \le 0$, which holds between the roots, end points included. So the rocket is at least $40$ m high for $[2, 4]$: from $t = 2$ s to $t = 4$ s.

(b) A height of at least $50$ m needs $30t - 5t^2 \ge 50$, that is $t^2 - 6t + 10 \le 0$. The discriminant is $36 - 40 = -4 < 0$, so $t^2 - 6t + 10$ has no real root and, with leading coefficient $1$, is always positive. So $t^2 - 6t + 10 \le 0$ has no solution and the height never reaches $50$ m. (The greatest height is $45$ m, at $t = 3$.)

questions.solution_md: Both parts reduce to a quadratic inequality in $t$.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts.

(a) Solve $\dfrac{3x + 1}{x - 2} < 1$ for real $x \ne 2$. [3]

(b) Find the real numbers $x$ that satisfy both $\dfrac{3x + 1}{x - 2} < 1$ and $4x - 3 \ge -5$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Subtract $1$: $\dfrac{3x + 1 - (x - 2)}{x - 2} = \dfrac{2x + 3}{x - 2} < 0$. The critical points are $-\dfrac{3}{2}$ and $2$. The fraction is negative when the top and bottom have opposite signs, that is between them. The strict sign leaves out both end points, and $2$ is excluded anyway. The solution set is $(-\dfrac{3}{2}, 2)$.

(b) The second inequality gives $4x \ge -2$, so $x \ge -\dfrac{1}{2}$. The common part of $(-\dfrac{3}{2}, 2)$ and $[-\dfrac{1}{2}, \infty)$ is $[-\dfrac{1}{2}, 2)$.

questions.solution_md: Part (a) needs one side zero; part (b) is a common part.

questions.stem_md:
The quadratic $x^2 - 2kx + 3k + 4$ has a constant $k$.

(a) State the condition on the discriminant for $x^2 - 2kx + 3k + 4 > 0$ to hold for every real $x$. [1]

(b) Hence find the set of values of $k$. [3]

(c) Verify your answer by testing $k = 0$ and $k = 5$. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The parabola opens upwards, so the expression is positive for every real $x$ exactly when it has no real root: $D < 0$.

(b) $D = (-2k)^2 - 4(1)(3k + 4) = 4k^2 - 12k - 16 < 0$, so $k^2 - 3k - 4 < 0$. Factorise: $(k + 1)(k - 4) < 0$, which holds between the roots. So $(-1, 4)$, that is $-1 < k < 4$.

(c) For $k = 0$ the expression is $x^2 + 4$, which is positive for all real $x$, as predicted since $0$ is in $(-1, 4)$. For $k = 5$ it is $x^2 - 10x + 19$, which equals $25 - 50 + 19 = -6 < 0$ at $x = 5$, as predicted since $5$ is outside the set.

questions.solution_md: Negative discriminant, then a quadratic inequality in $k$.

questions.stem_md:
Consider the two conditions on a real number $x$: $x^2 - x - 12 \le 0$ and $\dfrac{x + 1}{x - 6} < 0$.

(a) Solve the first condition. [2]

(b) Solve the second condition. [2]

(c) Write the set of $x$ satisfying both conditions. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $x^2 - x - 12 = (x + 3)(x - 4) \le 0$, true between the roots with both included: $[-3, 4]$.

(b) The critical points are $-1$ and $6$. The fraction is negative when its top and bottom have opposite signs, that is for $-1 < x < 6$. Both end points are excluded: $(-1, 6)$.

(c) The common part of $[-3, 4]$ and $(-1, 6)$ is $(-1, 4]$: $-1$ is out because the second condition is strict, and $4$ is in because both conditions allow it.

questions.solution_md: Solve each condition separately, then take the common part.

questions.stem_md:
A student solves $x^2 - 4x \ge 12$ as follows: "$x(x - 4) \ge 12$, so $x \ge 12$ or $x - 4 \ge 12$."

(a) Explain the error in this method. [1]

(b) Solve $x^2 - 4x \ge 12$ correctly. [3]

(c) Show with a number that the student's answer misses part of the solution. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The factor method is only valid when the product is compared with $0$. If $ab \ge 12$ it does not follow that $a \ge 12$ or $b \ge 12$ (for example $3 \times 5 = 15 \ge 12$ with both factors below $12$).

(b) Move everything to one side: $x^2 - 4x - 12 \ge 0$. Factorise: $(x + 2)(x - 6) \ge 0$. The critical points are $-2$ and $6$. The product is positive outside the roots and zero at them, so the solution set is $(-\infty, -2] \cup [6, \infty)$.

(c) The student's answer is $x \ge 12$ (the second case $x \ge 16$ adds nothing). Take $x = 7$: $7^2 - 4(7) = 21 \ge 12$ is true, but $7$ is not in the student's set. Also $x = -3$ gives $9 + 12 = 21 \ge 12$.

questions.solution_md: Always compare with zero before factorising.

marking_scheme.step: Error: factor method needs the right side $0$

questions.stem_md:
An imagined notice board is a rectangle of breadth $x$ cm and length $(2x + 3)$ cm. Its area must be at most $90$ square centimetres and its perimeter at least $30$ cm.

(a) Show that the area condition is $2x^2 + 3x - 90 \le 0$ and solve it for $x > 0$. [2]

(b) Form and solve the perimeter condition. [1]

(c) Find the whole-number values of $x$ that satisfy both conditions and the area of the board for the greatest one. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Area $= x(2x + 3) \le 90$, so $2x^2 + 3x - 90 \le 0$. Factorise: $(2x + 15)(x - 6) \le 0$, true for $-\dfrac{15}{2} \le x \le 6$. Since a breadth is positive, $0 < x \le 6$.

(b) Perimeter $= 2\bigl(x + 2x + 3\bigr) = 6x + 6 \ge 30$, so $6x \ge 24$ and $x \ge 4$.

(c) Both conditions give $4 \le x \le 6$, so the whole numbers are $4, 5, 6$. For the greatest, $x = 6$, the area is $6 \times 15 = 90$ square centimetres.

questions.solution_md: Area gives a quadratic inequality; perimeter gives a linear one; then combine.
